title: Grace perfects nature (ST I.1.8)
hook: grace doesn't destroy nature but brings it to completion

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the Summa works: objections, on the contrary, I answer that, and replies. Your line was state the other side first.

A piano tuner arrives at an old upright that hasn't been touched in years. She doesn't saw it in half or swap it for a synthesizer. She opens the lid, finds the strings and hammers already there, and works on them one by one, until it sounds the way it was built to sound. Same wood. Same keys. Only now, finished. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that works like that tuner. It's tucked into a reply early in the Summa, and it shapes how he holds faith and reason, God and the ordinary person. Today's word is that line.
screen: `AN OLD PIANO.` → `NOT SAWN IN HALF.` → `BROUGHT TO PITCH.`

segments.voice: It comes in the Summa's very first question, at the eighth article: does sacred teaching argue? Yes, Thomas says. Not to prove the faith, which rests on what God has revealed, but to start from it and make other things clear. Then an objection: if faith rests on God's word, doesn't bringing in human reason cheapen it? His reply, put plainly: grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it. So natural reason should serve faith, the way the will's natural leaning serves love. Nature is what a thing is made with. For a person: a mind that asks why, a body, a temperament, hands that can learn a craft. Grace is God's free gift. Thomas sets two pictures aside. In one, grace is a bulldozer: to be holy, stop being human. Flatten the mind, scorn the body. In the other, grace is a sticker, pasted on top, leaving you just as you were. Thomas's picture is the tuner: grace works on what's already there and brings it to completion. He shows it in the same reply. Paul, preaching in Athens, quotes the Greeks' own poets. In the Douay-Rheims, Acts gives his words: "as some also of your own poets said: For we are also his offspring." A pagan poet's line, put to work for the gospel. Reason wasn't thrown out. It was given a job. So Catholic teaching can say your curiosity, your humor, your patience with a tangled knot are not rivals to holiness. Catholics say grace takes them further than they could go alone.
screen: `DOES SACRED TEACHING ARGUE?` · `GRACE DOES NOT DESTROY NATURE.` · `NOT A BULLDOZER, NOT A STICKER.` · `PAUL QUOTES A GREEK POET.` · then, large: `FOR WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you were simply made with: a quick mind, steady hands, a good ear, a knack for putting people at ease, then a second and a third if they come. Notice you didn't earn them. If you pray, thank God for each one by name; if you don't, hold them a moment as things given.
Grace perfects nature. Thomas Aquinas's line from the Summa's first question: God's gift doesn't wipe out what we are, it brings it to completion.
Your line: grace completes. Not a bulldozer, and not a sticker either. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic teachers often use Thomas's line that grace perfects nature to explain why the Church values reason, science, art and ordinary human gifts alongside faith.

chat.meaning: In the Summa's first question Thomas writes that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, so natural reason serves faith.

Summa.meaning: Thomas Aquinas's great book of theology

Athens.meaning: the Greek city where Paul preached and quoted a poet

pagan.meaning: here, a Greek who worshiped the old gods

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old English Catholic translation of the Bible

notes: ST I.1.8 paraphrased: sacred doctrine argues from the articles of faith, not to prove them; reply 2: since grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity; Paul quoting a poet (Thomas names Aratus) at Acts 17:28. Confirm.

Original: Thomas's Latin is 'cum enim gratia non tollat naturam, sed perficiat'; the commonly cited form 'gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit eam' is a later summary. Confirm the form given and the pronunciation.
The bulldozer and sticker pictures are the script's own illustrations, not Thomas's.
'Catholics say grace takes them further' — confirm this fairly summarizes Catholic teaching on grace and natural gifts.
